directAnswer: Pope Paul II was Pietro Barbo, a Venetian nobleman and nephew of Pope Eugene IV, who reigned from 1464 to 1471. He is remembered for building the Palazzo San Marco (today's Palazzo Venezia), for his clash with Rome's humanist scholars, and for fixing the Jubilee year at every 25 years.

sections.h2: A Venetian Nephew of Eugene IV
paras: Pietro Barbo was born in Venice in 1417 into a merchant family whose fortunes rose when his maternal uncle, Gabriele Condulmer, became Pope Eugene IV. Originally intended for a commercial career, Pietro turned to the Church instead, and his uncle made him a cardinal while he was still in his early twenties.

As cardinal he became known for his wealth, his love of ceremony, and a remarkable collection of gems, coins, and antiquities. When the cardinals met after the death of Pius II in 1464, they chose him quickly. Before the vote they had all signed an election agreement meant to limit the new pope's power, but Paul II set it aside once in office, which soured relations with part of the Sacred College.

sections.h2: The Abbreviators, Platina, and the Roman Academy
paras: Paul II's most lasting controversy began when he dissolved the college of abbreviators, officials who drafted papal documents and whose posts many humanists had purchased. One of them, the scholar Bartolomeo Platina, protested loudly and was imprisoned. In 1468 the pope also moved against the Roman Academy of Pomponio Leto, suspecting its members of paganizing tendencies and of plotting against him; several were jailed and later released.

Because Platina went on to write the influential Lives of the Popes, Paul II's reputation has long been shaped by a hostile witness. Modern historians treat Platina's portrait of an anti-intellectual pope with caution, noting that Paul II also protected scholars and that printing took root in Rome during his reign, with the first presses at nearby Subiaco and then in the city itself.

sections.h2: Palazzo San Marco and the Carnival of Rome
paras: Even before his election, Barbo had begun a grand residence beside his titular church of San Marco. As pope he expanded it into the Palazzo San Marco, one of the first great Renaissance palaces in Rome, now called the Palazzo Venezia. He lived there for much of his pontificate.

Paul II also enlivened the Roman Carnival, sponsoring races along the street then called the Via Lata, which later took the name Via del Corso from those races. Critics saw this as worldly display; admirers saw a ruler who wanted Rome to feel like a capital again.

sections.h2: Bohemia, the Turks, and the Jubilee Cycle
paras: In foreign affairs Paul II confronted King George of Podebrady of Bohemia, who supported the Hussite compacts that Rome had rejected. The pope excommunicated and deposed him in 1466. He also tried, with little success, to rally Christian princes against the Ottoman advance after the fall of Constantinople.

In 1470 he decreed that the Holy Year should be celebrated every 25 years, the rhythm the Church still follows today. Paul II died suddenly of a stroke in July 1471, before he could see the 1475 Jubilee he had scheduled.

keyFacts: Born Pietro Barbo in Venice in 1417
Nephew of Pope Eugene IV, who made him a cardinal
Built the Palazzo San Marco, now the Palazzo Venezia, in Rome
Dissolved the college of abbreviators and imprisoned the humanist Platina
Set the Jubilee cycle at every 25 years (1470)
Died of a stroke on 26 July 1471

faqs.question: Why did Pope Paul II quarrel with the Roman humanists?
faqs.answer: He abolished the college of abbreviators, posts many humanists had bought, and later suspected members of Pomponio Leto's Roman Academy of conspiracy and pagan sympathies. Platina, one of those imprisoned, later wrote a harsh account of him that historians now read with caution.

faqs.question: What building in Rome is linked to Paul II?
faqs.answer: The Palazzo Venezia, originally called the Palazzo San Marco, which he began as a cardinal and expanded as pope. It is one of the earliest major Renaissance palaces in Rome.

faqs.question: Did Paul II change how often Jubilee years are held?
faqs.answer: Yes. In 1470 he fixed the ordinary Holy Year at every 25 years, the interval still used by the Church.
